q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE difference between Mongol rule in China and Mongol rule in Russia.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the Mongols governed China more directly than Russia, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which Mongol rule affected Russia's political development.

sample_answers.a: In China the Mongols established the Yuan dynasty and governed directly through a Chinese-style bureaucracy, while in Russia they ruled indirectly through the Golden Horde, leaving Russian princes in place as tribute-collecting vassals.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, China had a dense population and a sophisticated bureaucratic tradition the Mongols could take over and staff, while Russia's forests, distances, and smaller population made direct administration impractical — so the Mongols settled for tribute and obedience.
sample_answers.c: By destroying Kiev and elevating Moscow as their tribute collector, the Mongols helped Moscow accumulate power over rival principalities, laying the foundations for the centralized Russian state that emerged after the Horde's decline.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the Mongols' different approaches to China and Russia as adaptations to different conditions. In China, Kublai Khan conquered a populous, wealthy society with a two-thousand-year tradition of centralized bureaucracy; the Mongols simply took over this apparatus, placing Mongols at the top but employing Chinese officials to tax, administer, and govern. In Russia, the Mongols of the Golden Horde faced vast forests, great distances, and a smaller, poorer population; rather than administer directly, they demanded tribute and obedience, leaving Russian princes — especially Moscow's — to rule as their agents. The consequences diverged sharply: China experienced foreign dynasty but institutional continuity, while Russia's princes learned the arts of tribute extraction and autocracy that would shape the Muscovite state.
—Historian's account of Mongol rule in the period c. 1200–1450

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of Kublai Khan's court described by Polo.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Polo's account shows Mongol adaptation to Chinese traditions.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of Polo's account as evidence for how ordinary Chinese experienced Mongol rule.

sample_answers.a: Polo describes the khan's immense palace, his lavish ceremonies, and the vast administration of officials, messengers, and record-keepers that governed the empire.
sample_answers.b: Polo shows the Mongol khan performing the traditional Chinese imperial role — holding court, conducting rituals, and employing a Confucian-style bureaucracy — indicating that the conquerors adopted Chinese institutions to legitimize their rule.
sample_answers.c: Polo was a foreign merchant favored at court who saw only the splendor of the elite; his account ignores the heavy taxation, ethnic discrimination (Mongols ranked above Chinese), and resentment that most Chinese felt under foreign rule.

q2.stimulus:
The palace of the Great Khan is the greatest palace that ever was. The hall is so large that six thousand persons can sit at table. The Khan is served by barons and knights of his household, and all the business of the empire passes through his court. Messengers ride day and night along the post roads, and in every province there are officials who render account of revenues and justice. No monarch in the world has such power or such wealth, for all the riches of Cathay flow to his treasury.
—Adapted from Marco Polo, The Description of the World, c. 1300

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map of the Mongol Empire.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the Mongol Empire divided into separate khanates.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the division of the empire affected the regions under Mongol rule.

sample_answers.a: The map shows the empire at its height divided into four great khanates — the Yuan in China, the Golden Horde in Russia, the Chagatai in Central Asia, and the Ilkhanate in Persia — together covering most of Eurasia from Korea to Hungary.
sample_answers.b: Mongol succession custom divided territory among the khan's sons, and the empire's vast distances made centralized control impossible; after Mongke's death, rival claimants fought civil wars that permanently split the empire.
sample_answers.c: Each khanate adapted to its local conditions — the Yuan sinicized, the Golden Horde remained nomadic overlords, the Ilkhans converted to Islam — so Mongol rule produced divergent histories rather than a uniform empire.

q3.stimulus: The map shows the Mongol Empire at its greatest extent in the late thirteenth century, divided into four khanates: the Yuan dynasty in China, the Golden Horde in Russia and the western steppe, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, and the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Middle East. Together they formed the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from the Pacific to Eastern Europe.
